source.title: What the State Owes
source.summary: Government spending, public goods provision, and the dual model of bayt al-mal and waqf.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Once you collect taxes, how do you spend them? This episode examines government spending categories (defense, infrastructure, education, healthcare, transfers), the efficiency arguments for and against public provision, and the problems of bureaucracy, crowding out, and rent-seeking. The Islamic historical record shows a dual model: the bayt al-mal funded defense, infrastructure, and poverty relief directly, while the waqf system created a parallel, voluntary layer of public goods provision including hospitals, schools, and water infrastructure. Neither was perfect. The waqf system suffered from rigidity and eventual state capture under the Ottomans. But the institutional design, combining state and non-state provision, is worth studying on its own terms.

linkedin.post: Government spending raises fundamental questions: What should states provide directly, and what can emerge from voluntary coordination? The Islamic historical record offers an interesting case study. For centuries, Muslim societies operated a dual model: the bayt al-mal (state treasury) funded defense, infrastructure, and poverty relief, while the waqf system created a parallel layer of public goods provision. The waqf endowments built hospitals, schools, and water infrastructure without depending on tax collection or bureaucratic approval. Wealthy individuals and communities voluntarily funded public goods that served broad social needs. Neither system was perfect. The waqf suffered from rigidity—donors locked in specific uses that couldn't adapt to changing circumstances. The Ottomans eventually captured the entire system, turning voluntary provision into another arm of state control. But the institutional design itself—combining state and non-state provision—remains worth studying. It addressed both the efficiency problems of pure state provision and the coordination problems of pure market provision. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-trt-3

The endowments handled everything else through voluntary coordination, without depending on tax collection or bureaucratic approval. Neither was perfect. The waqf system suffered from rigidity as donors locked in specific uses that couldn't adapt over time. short_video.title: The Islamic Dual System for Public Goods
short_video.hook: The Islamic world solved public goods differently
short_video.voiceover: For centuries, the Islamic world ran a dual system. The bayt al-mal, or state treasury, handled defense and basic infrastructure. Meanwhile, waqf endowments created a parallel layer of public goods. Wealthy individuals voluntarily funded hospitals, schools, and water systems. No taxes required, no bureaucracy involved. The genius was institutional design: states did what only states can do, while voluntary coordination handled everything else. The system wasn't perfect. Endowments became rigid over time, and the Ottomans eventually captured the whole waqf system. But the model addressed both state inefficiency and market coordination problems simultaneously.
